item.title: Eight inmates granted Presidential pardons
item.description: Eight inmates have been granted presidential pardons, with five formally receiving their pardons in Suva today as they prepare to return to their families and communities. The Fiji Corrections Service said the pardons were presented during a ceremony led by the Acting Commissioner of Corrections.
item.content:encoded:
Eight inmates have been granted presidential pardons, with five formally receiving their pardons in Suva today as they prepare to return to their families and communities.

The Fiji Corrections Service said the pardons were presented during a ceremony led by the Acting Commissioner of Corrections.

The five inmates who received their pardons today are Aisake Qiolele, Josefa Tukana, Mohammed Harun Khan, Sailosi Rokotuiwalevu and Tang Lu.

The Acting Assistant Commissioner of Corrections Operations and the Southern and Central/Eastern divisional supervisors joined the Acting Commissioner in presenting the pardons and extending their best wishes to the recipients.

The remaining three pardoned inmates will receive their pardons at the corrections centres where they are currently held.

Luke Dikevitukana will receive his pardon at the Ba Corrections Centre, Mohammed Shaheen at the Lautoka Corrections Centre and Saula Rokobukai at the Labasa Corrections Centre.

Corrections officials told the recipients that their release should be viewed not as an end, but as a new beginning.

They were encouraged to carry forward the discipline and positive values developed during their time in the Corrections system and to make better choices as they reintegrate into society.

The pardoned inmates were also urged to maintain their faith and avoid returning to circumstances that could lead them back into incarceration.

The Fiji Corrections Service said the recipients now had an opportunity to rebuild their lives and reconnect with their families and communities.

They were encouraged to use their second chance to pursue lives marked by responsibility, purpose and positive change.

item.title: Church rejects racism claim
item.description: THE Methodist Church in Fiji and Rotuma has strongly rejected claims that race influenced the failure of Reverend Dr Anil Reuben to secure the positions of general secretary or president, but stopped short of explaining why the senior minister has not progressed to either of the church’s top leadership roles despite decades of service. item.content:encoded:
THE Methodist Church in Fiji and Rotuma has strongly rejected claims that race influenced the failure of Reverend Dr Anil Reuben to secure the positions of general secretary or president, but stopped short of explaining why the senior minister has not progressed to either of the church’s top leadership roles despite decades of service.

In a statement issued in response to claims circulating on social media, the church described the allegations as unfounded and misleading and called on police to investigate individuals it said were making statements capable of promoting division and destabilising the church’s reputation.

The controversy centres on claims that Dr Reuben, who has served the Methodist Church for about 50 years and currently holds the position of deputy general secretary, was overlooked for higher office because of his race.

The church, however, said Dr Reuben himself did not make the comments attributed to him online that he was not promoted because of his race.

“The MCIF wishes to make it absolutely clear that Rev Dr Anil Reuben did not make the comments attributed to him by this account regarding race,” the statement said.

While rejecting the race allegation, the church did not address the underlying question of why Dr Reuben has not advanced to the position of general secretary or president, despite his lengthy service and his current senior leadership role as deputy general secretary.

It also did not explain whether he had formally sought either position, whether he had been nominated or considered for the roles, or what factors have influenced previous leadership appointments.

Those unanswered questions remain at the heart of the wider discussion, particularly as the issue has now spilled into public debate over representation, leadership and advancement within one of Fiji’s major religious institutions.

The church instead focused on what it described as the damaging use of social media to circulate claims that could create division, confusion and tension in communities.

It said its name and the reputation of its deputy general secretary were being used by individuals to advance personal agendas and attract online engagement.

“Social media must not become a platform for individuals to pursue personal attention and engagement at the expense of institutions, their leaders and, ultimately, the peace and unity of our nation,” the statement said.

The church urged members of the public to verify information before liking, sharing or supporting posts containing unsubstantiated allegations.

item.title: School leaders told to watch for distress
item.description: GOOD mental health among teachers and students is essential when dealing with challenges in schools, says National Substance Abuse Advisory Council acting chief executive Josua Naisele. Mr Naisele made the remarks at the recent Fiji Head Teachers Association conference in Nadi.
item.content:encoded:
GOOD mental health among teachers and students is essential when dealing with challenges in schools, says National Substance Abuse Advisory Council acting chief executive Josua Naisele.

Mr Naisele made the remarks at the recent Fiji Head Teachers Association conference in Nadi.

He said school leaders needed to understand how to intervene when students or teachers faced challenges and recognise signs that they might need support.

Mr Naisele said some heads of schools referred teachers for counselling when they noticed symptoms of emotional or mental distress.

“Learning healthy coping skills – remember, it’s very important to identify healthy coping skills that you can apply when you start to feel these negative emotions,” he said.

He also stressed the importance of recognising the signs and symptoms of students experiencing challenges in their lives.

Mr Naisele said the council was also supporting selected primary schools through a mentoring program.

“We are engaging some of the retired teachers to become mentors in the selected schools,” he said adding that consistent support to students was important.

item.title: Alcohol in schools
item.description: STUDENTS are bringing alcohol to school in bottles and drinking it on school grounds, prompting a call for schools to strengthen and clearly communicate procedures for dealing with substance abuse. National Substance Abuse Advisory Council acting chief executive Josua Naisele said some students were using particular bottles to conceal alcohol before bringing it to school.
item.content:encoded:
STUDENTS are bringing alcohol to school in bottles and drinking it on school grounds, prompting a call for schools to strengthen and clearly communicate procedures for dealing with substance abuse.

National Substance Abuse Advisory Council acting chief executive Josua Naisele said some students were using particular bottles to conceal alcohol before bringing it to school.

“Reports from few schools of students who were using the stainless steel water bottle to fill alcoholic drinks and smuggle them to school,” Mr Naisele said.

“This is a concern as the children were so bold to do this knowing fully well it is not allowed.”

He also raised concerns about students taking vaping devices and illicit drugs onto school premises, adding that clearly defined procedures would help schools respond consistently and appropriately when such incidents occurred.

Mr Naisele made the comments while speaking to heads of school recently, where he urged school management and teachers to ensure staff and parents understood the steps to take when students were found with alcohol, vaping devices, tobacco or drugs.

Mr Naisele said prevention must begin with clear school policies aligned with those of the Ministry of Education, like the Child Protection Policy, Behaviour Management Policy, School Code of Conduct Policy, School Comforting Policy, and School Drugs and Substance Policy.

“These five policies are used to guide the teachers in addressing issues in school.”

item.title: Apted to lead panel
item.description: THE FMF Hibiscus Festival has announced its five-member judging panel for the 2026 festival, with lawyer Jon Apted appointed as chief judge. Mr Apted, a partner at Munro Leys, has practised law for 40 years and has previous experience in fashion, television and music competitions.
item.content:encoded:
THE FMF Hibiscus Festival has announced its five-member judging panel for the 2026 festival, with lawyer Jon Apted appointed as chief judge.

Mr Apted, a partner at Munro Leys, has practised law for 40 years and has previous experience in fashion, television and music competitions.

The panel also includes permanent secretary for Justice, Selina Camaibau Kuruleca, who also serves as acting permanent secretary for Women, Children and Social Protection and chairs the Fiji National Anti-Money Laundering Council. Pacific climate leader and narrative strategist Fenton Lutunatabua joins the panel, bringing more than 20 years of experience in climate action, communications, advocacy and regional partnerships.

Rotarian and former Rotary International District 9920 governor Vineeta Nand will also serve as a judge, drawing on her experience in banking, aviation, government, communications and public affairs.

Completing the panel is Miss Hibiscus 1975 Michele Smith, who was the last winner to wear the traditional Hibiscus crown before the introduction of the modern tiara.

Organisers said the judges’ diverse backgrounds would allow contestants to be assessed on areas including presentation, communication, character, cultural understanding and their ability to represent the festival.

item.title: Keep your ‘family intact’
item.description: MINISTER for Employment Agni Deo Singh has urged PALM Scheme workers to ensure their family units are intact despite the distances they will experience while working overseas. Speaking in Nadi recently, Mr Singh said the success of the labour mobility scheme should be measured not only by income earned overseas but by stronger families, better opportunities for children and lasting benefits for co
item.content:encoded:
MINISTER for Employment Agni Deo Singh has urged PALM Scheme workers to ensure their family units are intact despite the distances they will experience while working overseas.

Speaking in Nadi recently, Mr Singh said the success of the labour mobility scheme should be measured not only by income earned overseas but by stronger families, better opportunities for children and lasting benefits for communities.

Speaking at the opening of the Fiji Family Focus Workshop in Nawaka, Nadi, Mr Singh welcomed close to 100 returning and potential workers and family members.

He said Fijians often sought overseas employment to provide better education for their children, improve their homes, build savings and investments and create greater financial security.

However, he cautioned that financial gains should never come at the expense of family relationships.

“We must never allow temporary physical distance to become permanent emotional distance.

“Our children need love, guidance, discipline, protection and positive role models.”

He called on the workers to develop clear savings, investment, education and family plans to ensure every sacrifice made through overseas employment contributes to a better future.

item.title: Sewer leak hampers trashboom cleanup
item.description: A LEAKING sewer line is preventing the clean-up of a trashboom at Wailea, with accumulated rubbish now creating foul odours and health concerns for nearby residents. Trash Boom Pacific director Wayne Fuakilau said the Wailea trashboom could not be safely cleared because of health and safety reasons.
item.content:encoded:
A LEAKING sewer line is preventing the clean-up of a trashboom at Wailea, with accumulated rubbish now creating foul odours and health concerns for nearby residents.

Trash Boom Pacific director Wayne Fuakilau said the Wailea trashboom could not be safely cleared because of health and safety reasons.

“The Wailea trashboom has not been cleared due to a Water Authority of Fiji (WAF) sewer line discharging directly into the surrounding area,” Mr Fuakilau said.

He said Trash Boom Pacific discovered the leaking sewer on August 4 and reported it to the Ministry of Environment and Climate Change, asking that WAF address the problem.

“We remain unable to clear it until WAF resolves the issue,” he said.

He said the Wailea Settlement site was scheduled for weekly collection and the company had continued checking the site each week.

However, workers could not be sent into an area contaminated by sewage.

“I cannot risk the health and safety of our team by having them complete collections in a pool of leaking sewage until WAF addresses the issue.”

Mr Fuakilau said the sewer discharge was also responsible for the foul odour reported by residents.

Questions sent to WAF about the sewer leak and its response remained unanswered.

item.content:encoded:
THE amount of rubbish trapped by a new trashboom at Wailea has raised fresh concerns about the volume of waste entering Fiji’s waterways, with more than 75kg collected within its first six days.

Trash Boom Pacific director Wayne Fuakilau said the boom’s first collection on July 28 produced 75.69kg of waste — including 23kg of food packaging and soft plastics and 25kg of sanitary items such as diapers and sanitary pads.

“The system was installed on July 22, 2026. Our first collection on July 28, yielded 75.69kg of waste,” Mr Fuakilau said.

The figures provided an early snapshot of the waste flowing into the Wailea waterway and highlight the role of the trashboom in preventing rubbish from reaching the sea.

Mr Fuakilau said the system continued to intercept floating waste effectively despite the accumulated rubbish remaining at the site.

“The system continues to function effectively by intercepting trash, as you’ve seen.”

However, the boom has not been cleared since the first collection because the company discovered a leaking Water Authority of Fiji sewer line discharging into the surrounding area.

Mr Fuakilau said the leak created a serious safety concern for workers responsible for clearing the boom.

He said the Wailea site was scheduled for weekly collection after the initial 75.69kg haul.

Questions sent to WAF about the leak and its response remained unanswered.
